newsitem.title: UK: Britain to seek partners in aid.
newsitem.headline: Britain to seek partners in aid.

text.p: Britain's new International Development Minister said on Wednesday she would look for "partner governments" in developing countries to enhance the country's aid drive.
In her first major speech since taking the post earlier this month, Clare Short said such governments must be committed to creating the climate for aid to be effective.

"The effectiveness of what we are able to do through the aid programme depends not just on the size of our spend, but crucially on the policies and attitudes of developing country governments," she told London's School of Oriental and African Studies.
Short said aid could play a major role in supporting a momentum for economic reform in a country where the will already existed to implement it, but could not itself create the will.
"Partner governments must be committed to the creation of the right economic and political environment -- which includes dealing with corruption -- if sustainable development is to thrive," she said.
"We will be looking for such partners to work with."
Short said this would not mean imposing conditions on sovereign governments but looking for those with shared values.
"Where we cannot work with governments, we need to work round them, so that we can reach poor people even where the overall environment is unfavourable," she added.

But Short, the first British development minister for years to hold a seat in the cabinet, acknowledged that the election of a Labour government in Britain will not lead to an overnight increase in aid spending.
Labour fought the May 1 election on a pledge to maintain spending in each government department at the levels planned by the previous Conservative government for the next two years.
Short, an outspoken voice on the left of the centrist new government, pledged to knock hard on finance minister Gordon Brown's door to demand more aid spending after that.
"I am attempting to shift our spending towards a much more sharply-focused poverty eradication agenda in year two.
"I will then be in a position to ask for more resources in year three. I hope to be able to show that they will make a measurable difference," she said.

She noted that during the last 18 years of Conservative rule, spending on aid fell to 0.27 percent of Gross National Product from 0.51 percent. Labour is committed eventually to raising the figure to a United Nations target of 0.7 percent.
